statedGuarantee: Every agent tool invocation and every agent-to-agent delegation carries an Invocation-Bound Capability Token (IBCT): an Ed25519-signed, append-only chain that fuses identity, attenuated authorization and provenance. Block 0 fixes the ceiling of authority (scopes, budget in cents, max_depth, expiry); each delegating agent appends a block signed with its own key that may only narrow scope, budget and expiry and MUST carry a non-empty context string; the executing agent may append a completion block recording result hash, cost and verification status. A verifier resolves the issuer identity (aip:web via a signed .well-known document, or aip:key self-certifying), checks every signature in the chain, and evaluates Biscuit Datalog policies (Simple/Standard/Advanced profiles) against the requested tool, budget, depth and time. Verification is purely local with no authorization-server round trip. Bindings are defined for MCP (X-AIP-Token header), A2A (aip_identity / aip_token fields) and HTTP (Authorization: AIP <token>). The claim is that scope widening, depth violation, expiry replay, wrong-key verification, empty audit context and token tampering are all rejected, and that a completed IBCT answers who authorized an action, through which agents it flowed, under what constraints, and what the outcome was.
advertisedRhetoric: "Scope attenuation is cryptographically enforced: a delegation block that attempts to widen any capability beyond its parent block fails verification." and, in the threat model, "This is a cryptographic guarantee, not a runtime policy." The evaluation is reported as "AIP rejected 600/600 attack attempts across all six categories."
tierSpan: A verifier that skips signature checks, ignores policy evaluation, or accepts expired tokens can grant unauthorized access. AIP assumes the verifier is trusted and correctly implemented. Verifier compliance is an operational concern addressed through conformance testing and reference implementations, not a property the protocol can enforce cryptographically.
cheapestDefeat: Tier reasoning worked explicitly. GUARANTEE: an agent cannot exercise authority beyond the scope/budget/depth/expiry its token chain carries. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the resource-side AIP verifier -- the MCP server middleware that extracts X-AIP-Token, resolves the identity document, checks Ed25519 signatures and runs the Datalog authorizer. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: not forging a signature (Ed25519 forgery is infeasible, so the cryptographic layer holds on its own terms) but reaching the effector by a path that never presents a token to an AIP verifier -- calling one of the unauthenticated MCP servers the paper itself scanned ("A scan of approximately 2,000 MCP servers found all lacked authentication"), issuing a direct HTTP request to the tool's own endpoint, or performing the action locally (shell, file write, subprocess) where no verifier sits. The paper concedes the same failure from the other side: a non-compliant or dishonest verifier grants access, and "AIP assumes the verifier is trusted and correctly implemented." A second cheap defeat exists inside the protocol: aip:key sub-agent tokens have no holder binding ("Mutual authentication for self-certifying identities is deferred to v2") and real-time replay inside the TTL is unprevented, so a descendant handed the parent's token acts with the parent's full authority without ever appending an attenuating block. TIER OF THE DEFEATED MECHANISM: an application-layer chokepoint that binds only traffic which traverses it, i.e. T3. The cryptographic core is genuine and would be T1 for what a compliant verifier accepts, but under the weakest-link rule the enforceable boundary is the chokepoint -- exactly the worked example: forging the signature is unnecessary when the request can be made where nobody checks.
placementSpan: We evaluated AIP against six attack categories, with 100 iterations per attack (600 total attempts), under three deployment configurations: AIP (compact + chained), unsigned (no authentication), and plain JWT (standard signed JWT without AIP delegation semantics).

coverageSpans.E1: Clients include the IBCT in the X-AIP-Token HTTP header on every tool call.
coverageSpans.E2: AIP defines concrete bindings for three transport protocols, ensuring that a single identity and token format works across the agent ecosystem.
coverageSpans.E3: For generic HTTP APIs, the token is carried in the Authorization header using the AIP scheme: Authorization: AIP <token> .
coverageSpans.E6: For scenarios requiring immediate key compromise response, identity documents may declare a CRL endpoint, but no reference implementation enforces CRL checks.
coverageSpans.E7: Bounded depth. Block 0 declares a max_depth value (default: 3). Delegation beyond this depth is rejected.

schneider.surrogate: A monotone, monitorable safety property checked per invocation by a reference monitor (the AIP verifier): every block signature validates against a resolved identity document; each delegation block's scope, budget and expiry are a subset of its parent's; the declared depth does not exceed the authority block's max_depth; the token is unexpired; and every delegation block carries a non-empty context string. This is a prefix-closed safety property, and the 600-attempt adversarial suite tests exactly it.
schneider.objective: Accountable provenance -- the advertised claim that a completed IBCT answers "Who authorized this action? Through which agents did the delegation flow? What constraints applied at each hop? What was the outcome? Was the outcome independently verified?" -- plus the implied objective that granted authority is not misused. Neither is monitorable. Completion blocks are self-reported ("AIP provides attribution binding (the signature identifies who made the claim) but does not prevent a dishonest agent from misrepresenting results"), in-scope misuse is explicitly excluded ("a delegatee acting maliciously within its granted scope (e.g., calling permitted tools for harmful purposes) is out of scope for the token layer"), and colluding agents are not prevented. The truthfulness of an outcome record, and the absence of misuse, are not properties any single-execution monitor can decide.

notes: FULL TEXT OBTAINED from the arXiv LaTeXML HTML (v1, 25 Mar 2026, cs.CR; author Sunil Prakash, Indian School of Business). All spans are copied verbatim from that rendering; spans containing typographic apostrophes or inline-math artifacts were avoided when selecting quotes. CHARITABLE READING APPLIED: the paper is unusually honest and its own Sections 6 and 7 supply most of the downgrades, so the charitable and skeptical codings should converge on tier. The T1 case, which I considered and rejected under the weakest-link rule, is real and worth preserving for the adjudicator: Biscuit's append-only Ed25519 block chain plus check-all-blocks Datalog authorization genuinely makes scope widening cryptographically infeasible for a compliant verifier ("Scope attenuation is cryptographically enforced: a delegation block that attempts to widen any capability beyond its parent block fails verification"; 100/100 widening attempts rejected). It scores T3 because of placement, not cryptography: the check lives in server-side middleware (aip-mcp / aip_mcp, 151 and 76 LOC) reached only by requests that traverse it, and the paper's own motivating datum is that essentially no MCP server enforces anything. EFFECTOR MAPPING CAVEAT -- this is a protocol paper about authorizing tool invocations, not an agent-harness sandbox, so the ACTION-SURFACE-v1.1 effectors map obliquely; the coding is what the text supports, not a criticism of scope. E1/E3: the scope vocabulary is tool-namespaced (tool:search, tool:browse, tool:email), so a file-writing or network-fetching MCP tool invoked through an AIP-enforcing server IS bounded (rename/unlink would simply be further tool scopes), but writes and egress performed by the agent process itself, or by any descendant that does not route through such a server, are provably unreached -- hence partial, and the covert-channel rule alone would cap both at partial regardless. E2/E4/E5: process spawn, VCS push and package install (including install hooks and their network activity) are never mentioned; per the coding rules that is not-covered, not not-applicable, and I left the E4/E5 spans empty because there is no text to quote -- their absence from a paper whose surface is MCP/A2A/HTTP transports is itself the finding. E6: AIP replaces the ambient bearer credential for tool calls with a scoped capability, which is a charitable argument for partial, but it publishes no credential list and does not mediate the agent's access to env vars, config files, keychains or cloud metadata endpoints, and its own signing keys have no working revocation ("no reference implementation enforces CRL checks"); I scored not-covered and flag this as the cell most open to reasonable disagreement. E7 IS THE STRONGEST CELL and the one I most nearly scored covered: ephemeral sub-agents receive a generated Ed25519 keypair, an aip:key identity, a narrowed-scope delegation block and a minutes-long TTL, and max_depth genuinely reaches descendants -- a sub-agent's own sub-agent is rejected past the bound, which is real descendant mediation and the attack category (depth violation) that plain JWT misses. It remains partial because (a) spawning itself is ungated: fan-out breadth is unbounded and nothing in the protocol observes a spawn that never presents a token, and (b) a parent can hand its own unattenuated token to a descendant, which the paper leaves open by deferring holder binding for self-certifying identities to v2 and by conceding that real-time replay within the token's TTL window is not prevented by the token alone. EVIDENCE L2, not L3: reference implementations in Rust (1,214 LOC) and Python (827 LOC) exist at github.com/sunilp/aip under Apache 2.0, with 78 cross-language conformance tests, real HTTP transport and live Gemini 2.5 Flash inference, and behavioral confirmation of 600/600 rejections. It is not L3 because no reproducible bypass is demonstrated and, per the authors' own limitations, everything ran on a single machine over localhost with no production traffic. The 600-attempt suite tests only token-layer attacks against a compliant verifier; the bypass that determines the tier (never consulting a verifier) is not in the test matrix, which is why the headline 100% rejection should not be read as coverage. ADVERSARY PLACEMENT: primary A1 because every tested adversary acts on the token from outside the verifier's trust boundary (tampered base64, wrong-key signature, expired replay, a delegatee presenting a widened block; the attack table row reads "Agent invokes tool:email when only tool:search was delegated"). A4 is secondary, named but untested -- "Dishonest verifier" and "Colluding sub-agents" both appear in the Table 9 threat summary under Detected / Not Addressed and are never exercised. A5 is secondary via "Compromised identity host (DNS hijack)" and the DNS trust-anchor limitation: detected by the document self-signature, undefended if the attacker also holds the private key. A2 (adversary in inputs or retrieved context, i.e. prompt injection) is nowhere addressed -- an injected instruction that causes the agent to call a tool it legitimately holds scope for passes every AIP check, which is the honest boundary of a capability-token layer and worth stating explicitly in the SoK. TWO ITEMS FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: (1) the related-work Table 1 self-scores AIP as the only approach satisfying all seven properties, which is an artifact of the authors' own criteria and should not be recoded as evidence; (2) there is an internal date oddity in the bibliography -- self-citations dated 2025a/b/c carry 2603.* arXiv identifiers -- which affects none of the codings above.
